Summary:

This is a tour de force study that aims to understand the genetic basis of male germ cell development across three animal species (human, mouse and flies) by performing a genetic program conservation analysis (using phylostratigraphy and network science) with a special emphasis on genes that peak or decline during mitosis-to-meiosis. This analysis, in agreement with previous findings, reveals that several genes active during and before meiosis are deeply conserved across species, suggesting ancient regulatory mechanisms. To identify critical genes in germ cell development, the investigators integrated clinical genetics data, performing gene knockdown and knockout experiments in both mice and flies. Specifically, over 900 conserved genes were investigated in flies, with three of these genes further studied in mice. Of the 900 genes in flies, ~250 RNAi knockdowns had fertility phenotypes. The fertility phenotypes for the fly data can be viewed using the following browser link: https://pages.igc.pt/meionav. The scope of target gene validation is impressive. Below are a few minor comments.

(1) In Supplemental Figure 2, it is notable that enterocyte transcriptomes are predominantly composed of younger genes, contrasting with the genetic age profile observed in brain and muscle cells. This difference is an intriguing observation and it would be curious to hear author comments.

(2) Regarding the document, the figures provided only include supplemental data; none of the main text figures are in the full PDF.

(3) Lastly, it would be great to section and stain mouse testis to classify the different stages of arrest during meiosis for each of the mouse mutants in order to compare more precisely to flies.

This paper serves as a vital resource, emphasizing that only through the analysis of hundreds of genes can we prioritize essential genes for germ cell development. its remarkable that about 60% of conserved genes have no apparent phenotype during germ cell development.

Strengths:

High-throughput screening was conducted on a conserved network of 920 genes expressed during the mitosis-to-meiosis transition. Approximately 250 of these genes were associated with fertility phenotypes. Notably, mutations in 5 of the 250 genes have been identified in human male infertility patients. Furthermore, 3 of these genes were modeled in mice, where they were also linked to infertility. This study establishes a crucial groundwork for future investigations into germ cell development genes, aiming to delineate their essential roles and functions.

Weaknesses:

The fertility phenotyping in this study is limited, yet dissecting the mechanistic roles of these proteins falls beyond its scope. Nevertheless, this work serves as an invaluable resource for further exploration of specific genes of interest.

results.result: Male germ cells express approximately 10,000 protein-coding genes on average (9,468±498–12,195±1144 depending on species), corresponding to roughly half of the protein-coding genome (48.0–67.9%).
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C20 are well-supported by RNA-Seq data analysis across three species (human, mouse, fruit fly) using TPM >1 as the expression threshold, as shown in Figure 1b. The methodology is clearly described and the quantitative estimates are consistent across claims.

results.result: The majority (65.2-70.3%) of genes expressed in male germ cells are deeply conserved (phylostrata 1-5, common to all Metazoa), a proportion not significantly different from somatic cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C21, and C22 are supported by phylostratigraphy analysis shown in Figure 1d. The statistical comparison between germ cells and somatic cells is appropriate (Mann-Whitney U test), and the finding challenges the assumption that male germ cells have uniquely divergent transcriptomes.

results.result: Male germ cells have a more diversified transcriptome than somatic cells, but this increased complexity is mainly restricted to extremely low expression levels (TPM 0.01-0.5).
results.evaluation: Claims C18 and C19 are supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 1b. The observation that transcriptome diversity differences disappear at higher expression thresholds is important for interpreting the functional significance of the male germ cell transcriptome and suggests much of the apparent diversity may reflect transcriptional noise.

results.result: Between 49.7-63.4% of deeply conserved genes in male germ cells are ubiquitously expressed, suggesting that almost half are involved in cell-type-specific rather than housekeeping functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C24 are supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b. The inference in C24 logically follows from the data in C23, though the distinction between 'ubiquitous' and 'housekeeping' could be more rigorously defined.

results.result: The male germ cell transcriptome has an old evolutionary origin, with meiotic and pre-meiotic cells having older transcriptomes (lower TAI) than post-meiotic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C25 and C26 are supported by transcriptome age index (TAI) analysis shown in Figure 1e. The finding is consistent with prior work in mammals (Murat et al., 2023) and extends it to invertebrates, though the pattern is less clear in fruit flies due to residual post-meiotic transcription.

results.result: Deeply conserved genes in spermatocyte PPI networks are significantly more connected than non-conserved genes, and machine learning classifiers can reliably predict gene conservation based on network features (AUC 0.74-0.82).
results.evaluation: Claims C27 and C28 are supported by network analysis (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and machine learning analysis (Figure 1i). The Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests are appropriate, and the AUC scores indicate good predictive performance. Random edge shuffling experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 6) address potential ascertainment bias.

results.result: The orthoBackbone represents less than 3% of spermatocyte PPI network edges but contains 70% of deeply conserved genes, which are preferentially involved in gene expression regulation rather than cell signaling, with modest overlap (16.2-18.0%) between spermatocyte and enterocyte orthoBackbones.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are supported by orthoBackbone analysis (Figures 2b-d, Figure 1—figure supplement 3d). The methodology is novel and well-described. The GO enrichment analysis appropriately identifies functional differences between orthoBackbone and other conserved genes. The modest overlap with enterocytes supports cell-type specificity.

results.result: A subset of 79 functional interactions between 104 gene expression regulators represents a core component of the conserved genetic program of spermatogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C33 are supported by orthoBackbone analysis combined with GO term filtering (Figure 2e). The identification of this core network is a key finding, though the claim that it represents a 'core component' is somewhat interpretive. The number (104 genes) is consistent with prior estimates of conserved spermatogenic programs.

results.result: In vivo RNAi screening identified 250 conserved transcriptional burst genes (27.2% of 920 tested) essential for male fertility, with 76.0% being part of the orthoBackbone and 161 (64.4%) representing previously unknown spermatogenesis genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by systematic RNAi screening in Drosophila (Figure 2g-i). The experimental design is appropriate with proper controls, and the fertility threshold (75%) is justified. The enrichment of orthoBackbone genes among hits is statistically significant (Fisher's exact test p<0.0001). Literature searches to determine novelty appear thorough.

results.result: A homozygous loss-of-function variant in RNF113B (c.556_565del) causes meiotic arrest in humans, with spermatocytes being the most advanced cell stage in 89.0% of seminiferous tubules, phenocopying the dRNF113 RNAi in fruit flies.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are supported by genetic analysis, segregation studies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and histological analysis (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b). The phenotypic similarity across species is striking. However, the causal link would be strengthened by functional rescue experiments or additional affected individuals.

results.result: Mouse Rnf113a2 knockout mice are sterile with severely impaired spermatogenesis (SCO phenotype), and RNF113 proteins are predominantly expressed at meiotic entry with nuclear accumulation in spermatocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by mouse knockout analysis (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-g), single-cell RNA-Seq (Figure 3e), and immunofluorescence (Figure 3f). The cross-species validation strengthens the case for RNF113B as a conserved regulator of spermatogenesis.

results.result: Loss of RNF113 function disrupts 21.7% (human) and 20.3% (fruit fly) of testicular transcriptomes, affecting 30.0% and 26.3% of orthoBackbone edges respectively, with greater impact than Prp19 silencing (15.2% disruption).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 are supported by RNA-Seq differential expression analysis (Figures 3g-h, Figure 3—figure supplement 3). The comparison with Prp19 is appropriate as both are spliceosomal components. The statistical significance of the difference (Fisher's exact test p<0.0001) is properly reported. However, one human sample had low RIN (2.0), though DegNorm correction suggests minimal impact.

results.result: RNF113B loss disrupts 38.0% of the core spermatogenic program interactions, with significant enrichment of downregulated core genes (19.2% vs 10.0% genome-wide, p=0.0046), identifying 61 conserved genes downregulated in both human and fly, of which 27 had prior links to male fertility.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 are supported by comparative transcriptome analysis (Figures 3g, 3i, Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The statistical test (Fisher's exact) is appropriate. The cross-species overlap provides strong evidence for conserved downstream targets. Literature validation of the 27 genes appears thorough.

results.result: Two heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HSPA2 were identified in infertile men, with functional validation showing that silencing the fly ortholog (Hsc70-1) phenocopies dRNF113 meiotic arrest, and one patient (M2190) displaying SCO phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 are partially supported. The genetic variants are well-characterized (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), and functional validation in flies is convincing (Figure 3—figure supplement 5a-b). However, the evidence for autosomal dominant inheritance is incomplete—in silico predictions don't meet conservative thresholds, and only one patient has histology. The claim of 'new potential genetic cause' is appropriately cautious but requires additional validation.

results.result: Two heterozygous KPNA2 variants were identified in infertile men, including one de novo variant (c.667-2A>G in M1645), with functional validation showing post-meiotic defects in flies and SCO phenotype in one patient (M2098), making KPNA2 a strong autosomal-dominant candidate gene.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 are well-supported. The de novo occurrence (C64) provides strong evidence for pathogenicity. Functional validation in flies shows post-meiotic defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 6a-b), consistent with known functions. In silico predictions favor autosomal dominance more strongly than for HSPA2. The claim that KPNA2 is a 'strong' candidate while HSPA2 needs more data (C67) is appropriately nuanced.

results.result: Male germ cells share a common evolutionary origin, with gene expression identity maintained across species despite rapid evolution of reproductive genes, consistent with modular organization of biological processes and prior observations in plants and mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C17 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the conceptual framework for the study but don't represent novel findings from this work. The citations appear accurate and relevant to the claims made.

results.result: Deeply conserved genes play a prominent role in male germ cell regulation, with disruption of this ancient genetic program leading to human reproductive disease, and the transcriptional identity built around a small network of conserved interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 represent summary conclusions and interpretations. C68 and C69 are well-supported by the totality of evidence presented. C70 and C71 are more speculative interpretations (appropriately labeled as 'propose' and 'can be regarded as') that are consistent with but not definitively proven by the data.

results.result: Male infertility affects up to 12% of men, has a low diagnostic yield (30%), and only 104 clinically validated genes are known, highlighting a significant knowledge gap.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 provide clinical context supported by appropriate citations (Agarwal et al., 2015; Houston et al., 2021; Vissers et al., 2016). These establish the medical importance of the research but don't represent novel findings.

results.result: Male germ cells express approximately 10,000 protein-coding genes (at TPM >1 threshold), with 65.2-70.3% of these genes being deeply conserved (mapping to phylostrata 1-5 containing orthogroups common to all Metazoa). This percentage of deeply conserved genes is not significantly different from somatic cell types.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 states the work provides 'convincing evidence that a conserved core of functionally interacting genes lies at the basis of the male germ transcriptome.' Reviewer 3 notes 'this analysis, in agreement with previous findings, reveals that several genes active during and before meiosis are deeply conserved across species.' The data on gene expression thresholds and phylostratigraphy are treated as foundational and reliable.

results.result: Male germ cells have a more diversified transcriptome than somatic cells, but this increased complexity is mainly restricted to extremely low expression thresholds (TPM >0.01 to >0.5), suggesting transcriptional noise or other non-coding roles.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly acknowledges this finding, noting 'the use of a TPM >1 threshold for protein-coding transcripts...was a necessary compromise due to the high transcriptional noise of the system under study.' This indicates acceptance of both the observation of transcriptional diversity at low thresholds and the interpretation that it reflects noise. No reviewer challenges this claim.

results.result: Between 49.7-63.4% of deeply conserved genes in male germ cells are ubiquitously expressed (housekeeping), suggesting that almost half are involved in more specific roles beyond basal cellular functions.
results.evaluation: This finding is not questioned by any reviewer. The interpretation that non-ubiquitous conserved genes have specialized roles aligns with the reviewers' acceptance of the core genetic program concept. Reviewer 1 notes the work shows 'a conserved core of functionally interacting genes lies at the basis of the male germ transcriptome,' implicitly supporting specialized roles for conserved genes.

results.result: Meiotic and pre-meiotic cells have lower transcriptome age indices (TAIs) than post-meiotic cells across all three species, indicating older transcriptomes. The male germ cell transcriptome has an old evolutionary origin tempered by increased expression of younger genes at later developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'this analysis, in agreement with previous findings, reveals that several genes active during and before meiosis are deeply conserved across species, suggesting ancient regulatory mechanisms.' The TAI analysis is accepted as supporting evidence for the ancient origin of the spermatogenic program. No reviewer raises concerns about this temporal pattern.

results.result: Deeply conserved genes in spermatocyte PPI networks are significantly more connected than non-conserved genes (higher degree centrality and page rank), and machine learning classifiers can reliably predict gene conservation status based on network features (AUC scores 0.74-0.82).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 praises the 'experimental strategy that could also be applied to gene networks involved in different biological problems,' indicating acceptance of the network analysis approach and findings. The machine learning validation is not questioned by any reviewer, suggesting acceptance of the network-based conservation patterns.

results.result: The orthoBackbone represents only 1.7-2.7% of PPI network edges but contains 70% of deeply conserved genes. These orthoBackbone genes are preferentially involved in gene expression and protein regulation, with modest overlap (16.2-18.0%) between spermatocyte and enterocyte orthoBackbones.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the work 'shows that...a conserved core of functionally interacting genes lies at the basis of the male germ transcriptome,' directly supporting the orthoBackbone concept. Reviewer 3 notes the 'conserved network of 920 genes' and accepts the functional enrichment findings. The modest overlap with enterocytes supports cell-type specificity and is not challenged.

results.result: A subset of 79 functional interactions between 104 gene expression regulators, conserved across species and enriched in the orthoBackbone, represents a core component of the conserved genetic program of metazoan spermatogenesis.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the authors 'provide evidence for an ancient origin of the genetic program underlying metazoan spermatogenesis' leading to 'identification of a relatively small core set of functional interactions between deeply conserved gene expression regulators.' This directly affirms the core program concept. Reviewer 3 calls this 'crucial groundwork for future investigations.'

results.result: RNAi screening in Drosophila identified 250 genes (27.2% of 920 tested) essential for male fertility, with 76.0% being part of the orthoBackbone. Of these, 161 (64.4%) had never been previously associated with male reproduction, and at least 43.5% of the mitosis-to-meiosis transcriptional burst is required for germ cell functions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 emphasizes 'the scope of target gene validation is impressive' and notes 'High-throughput screening was conducted on a conserved network of 920 genes...Approximately 250 of these genes were associated with fertility phenotypes.' Reviewer 1 calls this a 'strength' and notes the work 'uncover[s] 161 previously unknown spermatogenesis genes.' The functional validation is accepted as robust.

results.result: 161 previously unknown spermatogenesis genes were uncovered through genetic interference with male germ cell identity in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the authors 'uncover 161 previously unknown spermatogenesis genes,' accepting this as a key finding. Reviewer 3 notes this work 'serves as a vital resource' and that 'about 60% of conserved genes have no apparent phenotype,' implicitly validating the novelty assessment. The claim is treated as a significant contribution.

results.result: RNF113B was identified as a cause of human male infertility through a homozygous loss-of-function variant causing meiotic arrest. The phenotype is conserved across species (human, mouse, fly), with RNF113B disruption causing widespread transcriptome deregulation (21.7% in human, 20.3% in fly) and disrupting 30.0% of orthoBackbone edges in human and 26.3% in fly.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the authors 'make a compelling case that...disruption of the male germ cell orthoBackbone can be exploited to identify new genetic causes of infertility.' Reviewer 3 notes 'mutations in 5 of the 250 genes have been identified in human male infertility patients' and '3 of these genes were modeled in mice, where they were also linked to infertility.' The cross-species validation and mechanistic data are accepted without challenge.

results.result: 61 conserved genes were similarly downregulated in both human RNF113B patient and fly dRNF113 RNAi, with 27 previously linked to male germ cell defects. Filtering for LoF variants in these 27 genes in a human infertility cohort revealed two new candidate genes: HSPA2 and KPNA2.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 confirms 'mutations in 5 of the 250 genes have been identified in human male infertility patients,' which includes HSPA2 and KPNA2. Reviewer 1 notes the work identifies 'three new potential genetic causes of human infertility' and that this demonstrates the utility of the orthoBackbone approach. The filtering strategy and candidate identification are accepted.

results.result: HSPA2 was identified as a candidate human infertility gene with two heterozygous LoF variants detected. The fly homolog Hsc70-1 silencing produces meiotic arrest equivalent to dRNF113, and one human patient (M2190) showed Sertoli cell-only phenotype.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept HSPA2 as a candidate gene (Reviewer 3 notes mutations were identified), Reviewer 2 notes 'the fertility phenotyping in this study is limited' and Reviewer 3 suggests 'it would be great to section and stain mouse testis to classify the different stages of arrest.' The manuscript itself states 'more data is still needed before drawing similar conclusions on HSPA2' compared to KPNA2, indicating incomplete validation.

results.result: KPNA2 was identified as a strong autosomal-dominant candidate gene for human infertility, with two heterozygous LoF variants detected including one de novo occurrence. The gene is required for post-meiotic development in flies and nuclear accumulation of Hop2 in mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the authors identify 'three new potential genetic causes of human infertility' and that the work makes 'a compelling case' for using orthoBackbone disruption to identify infertility genes. The de novo occurrence is particularly strong evidence that reviewers implicitly accept. Reviewer 3's comment about additional mouse phenotyping does not challenge the KPNA2 finding specifically but applies generally to all candidates.

results.result: Deeply conserved genes play a prominent role in male germ cell regulation, and disruption of this ancient genetic program leads to human reproductive disease. The transcriptional identity of metazoan male germ cells is built around a relatively small network of deeply conserved gene interactions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the work provides 'convincing evidence that a conserved core of functionally interacting genes lies at the basis of the male germ transcriptome' and that 'disruption of the male germ cell orthoBackbone can be exploited to identify new genetic causes of infertility.' The editor notes 'convincing data were presented and supported the main conclusion.' This represents the central thesis that all reviewers accept.

results.result: The shared genetic identity in metazoan spermatocytes can be regarded as a ramification of an ancestral multipotency program already present in germ line precursor cells.
results.evaluation: This interpretive claim is not challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 1 notes the work provides evidence for 'an ancient origin of the genetic program underlying metazoan spermatogenesis,' which aligns with this evolutionary interpretation. The claim is presented as speculation supported by citation and is consistent with accepted findings.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate C2 and C20 as SUPPORTED. OpenEval focuses specifically on RNA-Seq methodology and TPM thresholds. Peer review groups these claims with C3, C21, C22 in a broader assessment of conserved gene findings, treating the expression data as foundational without detailed methodological commentary.

Both evaluate C3, C21, C22 as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the phylostratigraphy analysis and statistical testing (Mann-Whitney U test). Peer review combines these with C2 and C20, focusing on the broader conclusion about conserved genes and agreement with previous findings rather than specific statistical methods.

Perfect agreement on C18 and C19 as SUPPORTED. Both recognize that transcriptome diversity differences disappear at higher expression thresholds and interpret this as reflecting transcriptional noise. Peer review explicitly acknowledges the TPM >1 threshold as a necessary compromise.

Perfect agreement on C23 and C24 as SUPPORTED. Both accept the finding about non-ubiquitous conserved genes having specialized roles. OpenEval notes the distinction between 'ubiquitous' and 'housekeeping' could be more rigorous. Peer review implicitly supports this through acceptance of the core genetic program concept.

Perfect agreement on C25 and C26 as SUPPORTED. Both accept the TAI analysis showing ancient conservation of pre-meiotic genes. OpenEval notes consistency with prior mammalian work and less clear patterns in fruit flies. Peer review emphasizes agreement with previous findings and ancient regulatory mechanisms.

Perfect agreement on C27 and C28 as SUPPORTED. Both accept the network analysis and machine learning validation. OpenEval provides detailed statistical assessment (Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, AUC scores). Peer review praises the experimental strategy's broader applicability without questioning the findings.

Perfect agreement on C29-C32 as SUPPORTED. Both accept the orthoBackbone concept and functional enrichment findings. OpenEval emphasizes the novel methodology and modest enterocyte overlap supporting cell-type specificity. Peer review explicitly affirms the conserved core concept and notes the 920-gene network.

Perfect agreement on C4 and C33 as SUPPORTED. Both accept the identification of a core spermatogenic program of 104 genes. OpenEval notes the claim is somewhat interpretive but consistent with prior estimates. Peer review emphasizes this as evidence for ancient origin and calls it crucial groundwork.

Perfect agreement on C34-C37 as SUPPORTED. Both accept the RNAi screening results and enrichment of orthoBackbone genes. OpenEval details the experimental design and statistical significance (Fisher's exact test p<0.0001). Peer review emphasizes the impressive scope and identification of ~250 genes with fertility phenotypes.

Both evaluate C38-C41 as SUPPORTED regarding RNF113B findings. OpenEval notes the phenotypic similarity across species is striking but suggests functional rescue would strengthen causal claims. Peer review groups these with additional claims (C6, C42-C50) in a broader assessment accepting cross-species validation without challenge.

Both evaluate C42-C44 as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes cross-species validation through mouse knockout, scRNA-Seq, and immunofluorescence. Peer review includes these claims in a larger group (R10) accepting the compelling case for orthoBackbone disruption identifying infertility genes.

Both evaluate C45-C48 as SUPPORTED. OpenEval details RNA-Seq differential expression analysis and notes one human sample had low RIN but minimal impact after correction. Peer review groups these with other RNF113B findings, accepting the mechanistic data and cross-species validation without specific challenge.

Both evaluate C49-C52 as SUPPORTED regarding conserved downstream targets. OpenEval emphasizes the statistical significance and literature validation of 27 genes. Peer review includes these in the broader acceptance of RNF113B findings and cross-species validation (R10).

Partial overlap on C51-C52. OpenEval evaluates these as part of RNF113B downstream targets (SUPPORTED). Peer review R11 focuses on the broader candidate gene identification strategy, accepting mutations in 5 genes including the filtering approach that leads to these findings.

Both evaluate C53-C59 (HSPA2 findings) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes incomplete evidence for autosomal dominant inheritance and limited histology. Peer review similarly notes limited fertility phenotyping and suggests additional mouse testis analysis. Both accept HSPA2 as a candidate but acknowledge incomplete validation, consistent with the manuscript's own cautious statement.

Minimal overlap on C53. OpenEval evaluates C53-C59 as UNCERTAIN due to incomplete validation. Peer review R11 accepts the broader finding that mutations in 5 genes were identified in infertility patients, treating the candidate identification strategy as SUPPORTED without specifically addressing HSPA2's validation status.

Perfect agreement on C60-C67 (KPNA2 findings) as SUPPORTED. Both emphasize the de novo occurrence as strong evidence. OpenEval notes functional validation in flies and stronger in silico predictions compared to HSPA2. Peer review accepts the compelling case for using orthoBackbone disruption to identify infertility genes, with KPNA2 as a key example.

Strong agreement on C68-C70 as SUPPORTED. Both accept the central thesis about conserved core genes and their utility for identifying infertility causes. OpenEval notes C70-C71 are more speculative interpretations. Peer review explicitly states 'convincing evidence' and 'convincing data were presented and supported the main conclusion.'

Both evaluate C71 as SUPPORTED. OpenEval treats this as speculative interpretation consistent with findings. Peer review accepts the evolutionary interpretation about ancient origin of the genetic program, noting it aligns with accepted findings and is not challenged by reviewers.
